voices.description: Measured and familiar; the default narration voice.
Clear and conversational for step-by-step instruction.
Warm and deliberate with distinct technical phrasing.
Direct and energetic without rushing terminology.
Steady and precise for commands and scientific terms.

selection.reason: Builds videos that do not require a live Neurodesk session.

videos.title: What is FSL?
videos.description: See how FSL's tools divide the work of inspecting, measuring, transforming, modeling, and reporting MRI data.

display.title: One toolkit, many jobs
display.body: FSL is a coordinated suite, not one giant application.

scenes.narrationText: FSL is a collection of focused neuroimaging tools. Instead of forcing every task into one program, it gives you different tools for viewing images, checking metadata, transforming data, fitting models, and reviewing results. Learning FSL means knowing which tool answers the question in front of you.

sourceRefs.note: Measurement framing and FSL lab goals

display.title: The job selects the tool
display.body: Viewing, modeling, measuring, and transforming are different operations.

items.label: Inspect
items.detail: See anatomy, overlays, and time series.

scenes.narrationText: Start with the scientific job. FSLEyes is for visual inspection. FEAT configures and evaluates fMRI models. Command-line utilities expose precise metadata, statistics, and image operations. These tools share a workflow, but they do not provide interchangeable evidence.

display.title: A report records the chain
display.body: FEAT links inputs, preprocessing, design, and statistical results.

visual.caption: A completed FEAT report organizes the analysis into reviewable stages.

scenes.narrationText: This FEAT report is one example of FSL's division of labor. FEAT organizes the model and its outputs, while visual checks often continue in the report and in FSLEyes. A completed report proves that software ran; it does not by itself prove that the analysis is scientifically valid.

display.title: Execution is not validation
display.body: Each tool produces evidence that still needs a scientific check.

items.label: Confirm the input
items.detail: Is this the intended image, run, and space?

items.label: Inspect the operation
items.detail: Does the setting match the analysis plan?

items.label: Read the output
items.detail: Does the result support the stated conclusion?

scenes.narrationText: A command can succeed on the wrong file. A model can finish with a poor design. An overlay can look plausible in one slice and fail elsewhere. Treat every FSL output as evidence to inspect, not as an automatic conclusion.

sourceRefs.note: Contrast and measurement depend on variability

scenes.narrationText: FSL is a suite of related tools. Choose the tool by the job, preserve the connection between steps, and inspect what each output actually demonstrates. Successful computation never replaces visual and scientific quality control.

sourceRefs.note: Measurement limits and FSL workflow goals

videos.title: How this course works
videos.description: Use a repeatable study loop that connects explanation, prediction, hands-on work, evidence, and reflection.

display.title: Understand, then operate
display.body: The course alternates explanation with observable work in FSL.

scenes.narrationText: This course is built around a simple loop. First understand what a step is supposed to do. Predict the result, run the step, inspect the evidence, and explain any difference between your prediction and what happened. That loop builds transferable judgment instead of button memory.

sourceRefs.note: Key-question structure used throughout the lectures

display.title: Make the result test you
display.body: A prediction turns software output into feedback about your understanding.

scenes.narrationText: Before running a command or changing a FEAT setting, state what you expect. A prediction makes the output diagnostic. If the output differs, the gap may reveal a path error, a misunderstood parameter, or a scientific assumption that needs revision.

sourceRefs.note: Questions and hypotheses drive design decisions

display.title: Use two working spaces
display.body: Keep the lesson visible while you work in Neurodesk or your approved FSL environment.

items.label: Workspace
items.detail: Your files, commands, and observed result

scenes.narrationText: Keep the explanation beside the working environment. Read one step, make a prediction, and then perform it yourself. Use a notes file to record commands, observations, and unresolved questions. The notes become part of your reproducible reasoning.

display.title: Expected output is a check
display.body: Compare after you have predicted and run the step yourself.

items.label: Copying
items.detail: Matches the example without testing understanding.

items.label: Comparing
items.detail: Explains why your result agrees or differs.

scenes.narrationText: An example is not an answer key to copy. Look at it after you have made a prediction and run the step. Then compare structure, not every character, because file paths and exact values may legitimately differ across environments and datasets.

Use each lesson as a cycle of understanding, prediction, action, inspection, and explanation. That habit is more valuable than memorizing a menu or command sequence, because it continues to work when the interface or dataset changes.

sourceRefs.note: Models should follow hypotheses about underlying processes

videos.title: Getting started with Neurodesk
videos.description: Choose an approved Neurodesk route, locate persistent storage, and distinguish the base shell from an FSL-enabled terminal.

display.title: Start in the right workspace
display.body: Neurodesk packages neuroimaging tools in a consistent software environment.

items.label: Access
items.detail: Use Play, EDU, or your institution's route.

items.label: Storage
items.detail: Find the location that persists between sessions.

items.label: FSL terminal
items.detail: Open the environment with FSL loaded.

scenes.narrationText: Neurodesk provides a consistent environment for neuroimaging software. Your access route may be Neurodesk Play, Neurodesk EDU, or an institutional deployment. The important first steps are to find persistent storage and open a terminal in which FSL is actually available.

display.title: Launch FSL deliberately
display.body: The app workspace separates general tools from software-specific environments.

visual.caption: The approved course image shows the Neurodesk application workspace and launcher.

scenes.narrationText: The application workspace gives you access to packaged tools. Open the FSL tile or the approved FSL terminal rather than assuming the base shell contains every neuroimaging command. The exact arrangement can vary, so identify the tool by its name and purpose rather than by memorizing a screen position.

sourceRefs.note: Approved course image of the application workspace

display.title: Ask the shell what it knows
display.body: A small command can confirm whether FSL is on the active path.

scenes.narrationText: Run which fslinfo in the terminal. A returned path means the shell can locate the program. If the command returns nothing, stop there. You may be in a base terminal, or the FSL environment may not have loaded correctly.

display.title: Temporary sessions can disappear
display.body: Save datasets, scripts, and notes only in the persistent location provided by your environment.

items.label: Session storage
items.detail: May vanish when the workspace stops.

items.label: Persistent storage
items.detail: Use for data, scripts, and written observations.

scenes.narrationText: Browser workspaces can contain temporary files that disappear when the session ends. Before downloading data or starting an analysis, identify the persistent storage location provided by your environment. Save your data, scripts, logs, and notes there, then verify that the files remain after reopening the workspace.

Begin every Neurodesk session by confirming three things: the approved access route, the persistent storage location, and an FSL-enabled terminal. Those checks prevent lost files and confusing command-not-found errors later in the workflow.

videos.title: The terminal
videos.description: Read a shell command as a precise instruction made from a program, options, and arguments.

display.title: A command has grammar
display.body: The shell separates a program, its options, and its arguments.

scenes.narrationText: A terminal command is a precise instruction. The first token usually names the program. Later tokens provide options and arguments. Spaces separate those pieces, capitalization matters, and the shell does not guess which file you intended.

display.title: Program, option, argument
display.body: Each token changes what the command does or which data it uses.

scenes.narrationText: Read the command from left to right. Here, ls is the program, dash l h adds detail and readable sizes, and data slash is the target directory. Changing one token can change the operation, the output, or the file being acted on.

display.title: Ask before you alter
display.body: Use non-destructive commands to confirm location and filenames first.

scenes.narrationText: Before running a command that creates or changes files, ask the shell where you are and what is present. P w d prints the working directory. L s dash l h lists its contents with useful details. Those two observations prevent many avoidable path errors.

display.title: Read the error literally
display.body: The message usually identifies a missing program, option, path, permission, or file.

items.label: Program found?
items.detail: Check the spelling and active environment.

items.label: Path correct?
items.detail: Print the directory and list the target.

scenes.narrationText: Do not respond to an error by changing several things at once. Read the message, identify the failing token, and test one explanation. Confirm the program, the current directory, the target path, and the option. Small checks make the cause observable.

A shell command is structured language. Identify the program, options, and arguments; verify your location and target; and use the output to test your understanding. Precision is the habit that makes command-line work reproducible.

videos.title: Linux navigation
videos.description: Use the working directory, absolute paths, and relative paths to move through a project without losing context.

display.title: Your location gives paths meaning
display.body: Relative paths begin from the directory where the shell is currently working.

scenes.narrationText: The shell always has a working directory. A relative path is interpreted from that location. An absolute path begins at the filesystem root. Many missing-file errors happen because the file is real, but the command is looking from the wrong context.

display.title: Absolute versus relative
display.body: Both can identify the same file, but they begin from different places.

scenes.narrationText: An absolute path states the full route from the root slash. A relative path states the route from where you are now. Relative paths are shorter and portable inside a project, but they only work when the starting context is correct.

display.title: Print, list, then move
display.body: Use one command to locate yourself, one to inspect, and one to change context.

scenes.narrationText: Use p w d to print your location, l s to inspect what is available, and c d to change directories. After moving, print the location again. This sequence turns an assumed path into observable evidence.

display.title: Check context before syntax
display.body: A correct command can fail when it starts from the wrong directory.

items.label: List the parent
items.detail: Verify each folder in the route.

scenes.narrationText: When a file cannot be found, do not repeatedly rewrite the command. Confirm the working directory, list the expected parent folder, and verify each part of the path. If needed, search within the project rather than across the whole system.

display.title: Location is part of the command

scenes.narrationText: Navigation is not separate from analysis. Your working directory determines how relative paths are interpreted. Print the context, inspect the route, and move deliberately so every later FSL command acts on the intended data.

videos.title: What is a NIfTI image?
videos.description: Build a NIfTI image from voxels, slices, volumes, and time while keeping spatial sampling separate from anatomical certainty.

display.title: A NIfTI stores sampled space
display.body: MRI data are organized as voxels, volumes, and sometimes time.

scenes.narrationText: A NIfTI file stores numerical samples arranged in space. One sample is a voxel, a tiny three-dimensional box. Voxels form slices, slices form a three-dimensional volume, and repeated volumes form a four-dimensional fMRI time series.

sourceRefs.note: Voxel, volume, run, and analysis hierarchy

display.title: Voxel, volume, time
display.body: The fourth dimension orders repeated 3-D measurements across the run.

scenes.narrationText: An anatomical image is often one three-dimensional volume. A BOLD image usually contains many volumes sampled at successive time points. The file header records dimensions, voxel sizes, orientation transforms, and timing so software can interpret the array correctly.

display.title: Dimensions describe the container
display.body: Inspect size, voxel spacing, and time points before interpreting intensities.

scenes.narrationText: Fslinfo exposes the image header. Here, the first three dimensions describe a sixty-four by sixty-four by forty spatial grid. Dimension four contains two hundred forty time points, and pixdim four reports a two-second repetition time. These values describe sampling, not data quality.

display.title: Smaller voxels are not automatically better
display.body: Spatial sampling, signal-to-noise, and functional localization are different properties.

items.label: Voxel size
items.detail: The dimensions of each measured box.

items.label: Functional resolution
items.detail: How precisely activity relates to a process.

scenes.narrationText: Voxel dimensions define spatial sampling, not anatomical precision. Smaller voxels can reduce signal-to-noise, and functional localization also depends on physiology, preprocessing, and experimental design. Never translate voxel size directly into certainty about a cognitive process.

sourceRefs.note: Spatial and functional resolution are distinct

scenes.narrationText: A NIfTI image is a structured numerical container. Understand its voxels, volumes, dimensions, orientation, and timing before analyzing intensity values. Sampling describes how data were arranged; it does not guarantee what the data can reveal.

videos.title: Understanding BIDS
videos.description: Use BIDS folders and filename entities to identify participants, tasks, runs, modalities, events, and metadata without local guesswork.

display.title: Structure is part of the data
display.body: BIDS makes files understandable to people and software through predictable names.

scenes.narrationText: The Brain Imaging Data Structure, or BIDS, uses predictable folders and filename entities. Those labels tell people and software which participant, session, task, run, and modality a file represents. The structure reduces ambiguity and makes automated workflows safer.

display.title: Entities answer specific questions
display.body: Each key-value pair identifies one part of the acquisition.

scenes.narrationText: Read a BIDS filename as a sequence of questions. Sub identifies the participant label. Task identifies the paradigm. Run distinguishes repeated acquisitions. The suffix, such as bold or T one w, identifies the data type. Underscores separate entities; hyphens separate keys from values.

display.title: Image, events, metadata
display.body: A functional run is interpreted with its matching events table and JSON sidecar.

scenes.narrationText: A functional NIfTI does not stand alone. Its matching events table describes what happened during the run, and the JSON sidecar records acquisition metadata. Shared entities in the filenames let you connect those files without relying on memory.

display.title: Identifiers do not belong in filenames
display.body: Use study labels rather than names, medical-record numbers, or other direct identifiers.

items.label: Direct identity
items.detail: Names and record numbers expose participants.

items.label: Study label
items.detail: A coded participant label supports de-identification.

scenes.narrationText: BIDS structure supports responsible sharing only when participant labels are de-identified. Do not place names, medical-record numbers, or other direct identifiers in filenames. Brain images may also require defacing and institutional review before they are shared.

sourceRefs.note: Private health information and MRI anonymization

display.title: Let the name explain the file

scenes.narrationText: BIDS makes file identity explicit. Decode the entities, follow shared labels across images, events, and metadata, and protect participant identity. Good structure is not cosmetic; it is part of reproducible and responsible analysis.

videos.title: Introduction to FSLEyes
videos.description: Use FSLEyes to inspect image orientation, coverage, intensity, and overlay order across three anatomical planes.

source.section: Viewing MRI data and functional time series

display.title: Looking is part of analysis
display.body: FSLEyes makes geometry, coverage, intensity, and alignment directly observable.

scenes.narrationText: Visual inspection is an analysis step, not decoration. FSLEyes shows the same coordinate in sagittal, coronal, and axial planes. It lets you inspect orientation, brain coverage, image intensity, and the relationship between overlays before trusting a pipeline result.

sourceRefs.section: Viewing MRI data and functional time series

display.title: Crosshairs connect the planes
display.body: Moving one view updates the same anatomical coordinate in the other two.

visual.caption: The approved FSLEyes image shows orthographic views, overlays, and a time-series panel.

scenes.narrationText: The orthographic display shows three views of one location. Crosshairs connect those planes, so a movement in one view updates the others. The overlay list controls which images are visible, their order, opacity, and color mapping.

sourceRefs.section: Viewing MRI data and functional time series

display.title: Check orientation and coverage
display.body: Look through the whole brain before preprocessing or modeling.

visual.caption: Inspect multiple slices rather than accepting the central view alone.

scenes.narrationText: Scroll from one end of the brain to the other. Confirm that left and right orientation are understood, the expected anatomy is covered, and no large region is missing or severely distorted. A later analysis cannot recover anatomy that was never acquired.

sourceRefs.note: Visual quality assurance and motion artifacts

sourceRefs.section: Viewing MRI data and functional time series

display.title: Plausible is not aligned
display.body: Central overlap can hide failures near frontal, posterior, superior, or inferior boundaries.

items.label: Inspect boundaries
items.detail: Follow cortex, ventricles, and major landmarks.

items.label: Inspect many slices
items.detail: Check the whole volume, not one center image.

items.label: Adjust display
items.detail: Opacity and contrast should reveal disagreement.

scenes.narrationText: Two images can overlap near the center and still be misregistered elsewhere. Inspect multiple slices and anatomical boundaries. Adjust opacity and color mapping so disagreement is visible. A reassuring first impression is not a quality-control result.

sourceRefs.section: Viewing MRI data and functional time series

scenes.narrationText: Use FSLEyes to understand the image before relying on derived results. Orient yourself in three planes, inspect coverage across the volume, and compare overlays at visible boundaries. Visual evidence is a required part of quality control.

sourceRefs.section: Viewing MRI data and functional time series

videos.title: Overlays, atlases, and time series
videos.description: Combine aligned overlays, voxel time series, and probabilistic atlas labels without treating any one view as ground truth.

source.section: Navigating anatomy, functional data, and atlas tools

display.title: One coordinate, several questions
display.body: Overlays show space, time series show change, and atlases provide probabilistic labels.

items.label: Overlay
items.detail: Compare images in the same space.

scenes.narrationText: A single coordinate can support several observations. Overlays compare spatial relationships. A time-series plot shows how signal changes across volumes. An atlas lookup supplies a reference label. These sources complement one another, but none should be treated as unquestionable ground truth.

sourceRefs.section: Navigating anatomy, functional data, and atlas tools

display.title: Overlay order changes what you see
display.body: Opacity, color map, and display range can reveal or conceal disagreement.

visual.caption: FSLEyes combines orthographic overlays with a signal plot at the selected location.

scenes.narrationText: The upper overlay can hide the image beneath it. Use opacity, color maps, and display ranges to expose boundaries in both images. A good display does not make alignment true; it makes agreement and disagreement easier to inspect.

sourceRefs.section: Navigating anatomy, functional data, and atlas tools

display.title: A voxel is a time series
display.body: In 4-D data, the selected spatial sample has one value for every volume.

visual.caption: The time-series panel plots the selected location across the run.

scenes.narrationText: In a four-dimensional BOLD image, each voxel contains a sequence of values. The plot shows that sequence across the run. Spikes, slow drift, and task-related structure are different patterns; seeing a change does not yet identify its cause.

sourceRefs.note: Signal size and sources of variability

sourceRefs.section: Navigating anatomy, functional data, and atlas tools

display.title: A label is a reference
display.body: Atlas boundaries summarize populations and may not match one participant exactly.

items.label: Coordinate
items.detail: The selected location in the displayed space.

items.label: Probability
items.detail: How consistently an atlas assigns a label.

items.label: Participant
items.detail: Individual anatomy can differ from the atlas.

scenes.narrationText: An atlas label is a reference derived from a template or population. It may be probabilistic, and individual anatomy varies. Confirm the coordinate space, inspect the participant's anatomy, and report uncertainty rather than presenting an atlas boundary as exact truth.

sourceRefs.section: Navigating anatomy, functional data, and atlas tools

scenes.narrationText: Use overlays, time series, and atlas labels together. Confirm spatial alignment, inspect temporal behavior, and keep atlas uncertainty visible. A defensible interpretation states what each view contributes and what it cannot establish.

sourceRefs.section: Navigating anatomy, functional data, and atlas tools

videos.title: fslinfo and fslstats
videos.description: Separate image metadata from value summaries and make the contributing voxel set explicit before interpreting a number.

display.title: Container facts versus voxel values
display.body: Fslinfo describes the image; fslstats summarizes selected intensities.

scenes.narrationText: Fslinfo and fslstats answer different questions. Fslinfo reads the NIfTI header and describes the image container. Fslstats calculates summaries from voxel values. A statistic is meaningful only when you know which image and which voxels contributed to it.

sourceRefs.note: fMRI signal is small relative to variability
Purpose and interpretation of statistical summaries

display.title: Metadata and statistics differ
display.body: Dimensions describe arrangement; statistics describe values inside a selected voxel set.

items.label: fslstats
items.detail: Mean, range, percentiles, and voxel volume.

scenes.narrationText: Use fslinfo when the question is about structure: dimensions, voxel spacing, orientation, or timing. Use fslstats when the question is about intensity values. The two outputs complement one another, but one cannot substitute for the other.

sourceRefs.note: Contrast, voxel size, and temporal sampling

display.title: State what was measured
display.body: Pair every reported value with the image, mask, threshold, and option that produced it.

scenes.narrationText: With dash V, fslstats reports the number of nonzero voxels followed by their physical volume in cubic millimetres. Those values describe the selected image. They do not automatically describe the whole brain, because zeros, thresholds, and masks determine which voxels are counted.

sourceRefs.note: Changing the basis of a statistical summary with an ROI

display.title: Make the voxel set visible
display.body: A precise statistic can still summarize the wrong anatomy.

items.label: Inspect the mask
items.detail: Overlay it on the exact source image.

items.label: Name the operation
items.detail: Record thresholds and options with the value.

scenes.narrationText: A numerical result can be perfectly computed and scientifically wrong. Confirm the input image and coordinate space. If a mask is involved, overlay it on the exact source data. Record the option and threshold so another person can reproduce the voxel set.

Use fslinfo to understand the image container and fslstats to summarize values. Never report a number without the image, option, threshold, and voxel selection that define it. Context turns output into interpretable evidence.

sourceRefs.note: Statistics assess data quality and hypotheses

videos.title: fslmaths and fslmeants
videos.description: Transform an image, inspect the resulting mask, and then extract a mean time series from spatially compatible data.

source.section: Measuring the brain and atlas masks

display.title: Transform first, measure second
display.body: Fslmaths creates an image; fslmeants extracts a time series from selected voxels.

scenes.narrationText: Fslmaths and fslmeants often appear together, but they do different jobs. Fslmaths applies operations in sequence and writes a new image. Fslmeants uses a mask to summarize a four-dimensional time series across selected voxels.

sourceRefs.note: ROI-based measurement changes the basis of a summary

sourceRefs.section: Measuring the brain and atlas masks

display.title: Operations run left to right
display.body: Each fslmaths option acts on the result of the previous option.

scenes.narrationText: Fslmaths reads an input, applies operations from left to right, and writes an output. A threshold removes values below a cutoff. Binarization converts the remaining selection to ones. The output is a new mask, not a label permanently attached to the original image.

sourceRefs.section: Measuring the brain and atlas masks

display.title: Make the spatial choice explicit
display.body: The mask defines which voxel time series enter the mean.

visual.code:
fslmaths zstat1 -thr 2.3 -bin roi_mask
fslmeants -i filtered_func_data -m roi_mask -o roi.txt
visual.output: roi.txt: one mean value per volume

scenes.narrationText: This example thresholds a statistical image, binarizes the result, and saves a mask. Fslmeants then extracts the mean BOLD value inside that mask for every volume. The output is a time series whose meaning depends entirely on the mask and source image.

sourceRefs.section: Measuring the brain and atlas masks

display.title: Matching dimensions are not enough
display.body: The mask and BOLD image must also represent the same spatial location.

items.label: Check dimensions
items.detail: Grid sizes and voxel spacing must be compatible.

items.label: Check transforms
items.detail: Headers should describe the intended space.

items.label: Check the overlay
items.detail: The mask must cover the intended anatomy.

scenes.narrationText: Two files can share dimensions while representing different anatomy. Check the headers, then overlay the mask on the exact image used for extraction. Confirm coverage across slices. A time series extracted from the wrong space is precise but meaningless.

sourceRefs.section: Measuring the brain and atlas masks

scenes.narrationText: Use fslmaths to create a derived image and fslmeants to measure a time series within a mask. Preserve the operation order, inspect the mask in the source space, and only then interpret the extracted values.

sourceRefs.section: Measuring the brain and atlas masks

videos.title: What first-level analysis means
videos.description: Model one participant's single run at every voxel and keep that scope distinct from within-subject and population inference.

display.title: One participant, one run
display.body: First-level analysis links one BOLD time series to one design at every voxel.

scenes.narrationText: A first-level analysis models one run from one participant. At every voxel, it compares the observed BOLD time series with predicted task and nuisance patterns. The resulting estimates belong to that run; they are not yet evidence about a population.

sourceRefs.note: Analysis hierarchy from voxel to group
GLM relationship between voxel data and hypotheses

display.title: Fit the design at every voxel
display.body: The design stays fixed while the measured time series changes across space.

scenes.narrationText: The design matrix describes expected patterns across the run. FEAT fits that same set of predictors separately to each voxel's measured time series. Beta estimates describe the fitted contribution of each column, and residuals contain structure the model did not explain.

display.title: Columns must match the run
display.body: Timing, confounds, and contrast weights should describe this exact acquisition.

visual.caption: The FEAT design matrix makes predictor timing and relative structure visible.

scenes.narrationText: Before interpreting a first-level result, inspect the design matrix. Confirm that task columns match the run's timing, nuisance columns have the expected length, and contrasts point to the intended explanatory variables. A design from another run can fit without answering the correct question.

sourceRefs.note: Contrasts, nuisance regressors, and column dependence

display.title: A run is not a population
display.body: Higher-level models are required to combine runs and generalize across participants.

scenes.narrationText: First-level results describe one run. Fixed-effects combinations can summarize multiple runs from a participant, but they still do not model population variability. Random-effects analysis uses variation across participants to support population-level inference.

display.title: Keep the level explicit
bullets: Fit the GLM voxel by voxel

scenes.narrationText: First-level analysis fits one run from one participant at every voxel. Inspect the design and contrasts in that scope, then use appropriate higher-level models for within-subject combinations and population inference. Never let the image hide the level of analysis.

videos.title: What is a GLM?
videos.description: Build the fMRI general linear model from observed BOLD signal, predictor columns, fitted estimates, and residual error.

display.title: Explain signal with a design
display.body: The GLM represents measured BOLD as modeled predictors plus residuals.

scenes.narrationText: The general linear model represents a measured BOLD time series as a weighted combination of predictors plus residual error. In compact form, Y equals X beta plus epsilon. FEAT fits this relationship separately at every voxel.

display.title: Four parts, four meanings
display.body: Observed data, design, estimates, and residuals must remain conceptually separate.

scenes.narrationText: Y is the observed BOLD time series. X is the design matrix containing task and nuisance predictors. Beta contains the fitted contribution of each column. Epsilon contains the remaining structure. Residuals are unexplained by the model; they are not automatically random or harmless.

display.title: The design encodes the hypothesis
display.body: Column order, timing, scaling, and dependence determine how estimates are interpreted.

visual.caption: The FEAT design matrix is the visible representation of X.

scenes.narrationText: The design matrix is not a decorative preview. Its columns encode the model. Confirm the timing, identify task and nuisance regressors, and look for strong dependence between columns. Beta estimates are conditional on all the other predictors in X.

display.title: A fit can answer the wrong question
display.body: Good computation cannot rescue a design that misrepresents the hypothesis or noise structure.

items.label: Hypothesis first
items.detail: Columns should represent the proposed processes.

items.label: Residuals inspected
items.detail: Look for drift, spikes, or other remaining structure.

scenes.narrationText: A GLM can fit successfully and still answer the wrong scientific question. The model should follow the hypothesis about underlying processes, not merely every stimulus label. Nuisance structure must be addressed, and residual patterns should be inspected rather than dismissed as noise.

sourceRefs.note: Regressors versus contrasts and hypothesis-driven modeling

display.title: The model makes assumptions visible
bullets: X and β encode the fit

scenes.narrationText: The fMRI GLM separates measured data, modeled predictors, fitted estimates, and residuals. Read those parts distinctly, inspect the design before the results, and remember that a successful fit only supports claims represented by the model.

videos.title: Experimental timing files
videos.description: Translate experimental events into FSL onset-duration-amplitude rows while preserving the design's detection and estimation goals.

display.title: Events become model input
display.body: FSL timing files encode when a condition starts, how long it lasts, and its amplitude.

scenes.narrationText: Experimental timing files translate the task into model input. Each row states an onset in seconds, a duration in seconds, and an amplitude. Each condition usually receives its own file so the design can form a separate explanatory variable.

display.title: Onset, duration, amplitude
display.body: Every row describes one modeled event or block in scanner time.

items.label: Duration
items.detail: How long the modeled input lasts.

items.label: Amplitude
items.detail: Its modeled height or parametric value.

scenes.narrationText: The first column is onset measured from the start of the run. The second is duration. The third is amplitude, often one for a simple condition but variable for parametric designs. These values describe the neural-event model before convolution with the hemodynamic response.

display.title: Timing must fit the run
display.body: Onsets, durations, and amplitudes should agree with the event table and scan length.

scenes.narrationText: Read each row against the event table. Confirm the units are seconds, not volumes. Check that onsets are nonnegative, durations are plausible, and no event extends beyond the run. Then plot or preview the resulting model rather than trusting the text file alone.

sourceRefs.note: Timing influences the hemodynamic model and efficiency

display.title: Timing changes what you can estimate
display.body: Blocked and jittered event-related designs emphasize different scientific goals.

items.label: Blocked
items.detail: Strong sustained differences, limited event separation.

items.label: Jittered events
items.detail: Separates trials and response shapes more flexibly.

items.label: Mixed
items.detail: Models sustained and transient effects together.

scenes.narrationText: Timing is part of experimental design, not file formatting. Blocked designs often provide strong detection power. Jittered event-related designs improve separation and estimation of individual events. Mixed designs can model sustained and transient effects. The best choice depends on the hypothesis and constraints.

A three-column file is a compact model of the experiment. Encode onset, duration, and amplitude accurately; validate the rows against the run; and remember that timing determines which effects the design can detect and estimate.

videos.title: What is an explanatory variable?
videos.description: Treat an explanatory variable as one hypothesized pattern in the design matrix and distinguish task, parametric, and nuisance meanings.

display.title: One column, one modeled pattern
display.body: An explanatory variable represents variation expected to explain part of the BOLD signal.

scenes.narrationText: An explanatory variable, or EV, is one modeled pattern in the design matrix. A task EV represents an experimental condition. A parametric EV represents graded trial values. A nuisance EV represents structured variation that is not the effect of interest.

sourceRefs.note: Design matrix, regressors, and categorical versus parametric predictors

display.title: Columns are not interchangeable
display.body: Two EVs can look similar but support different interpretations.

scenes.narrationText: The interpretation of an EV comes from how it was constructed and why it belongs in the model. A condition column asks about an average task effect. A parametric column asks whether response changes with a value. A motion column controls nuisance variation rather than testing the task.

sourceRefs.note: Regressors and hypotheses about cognitive processes

display.title: Verify order, timing, and dependence
display.body: Every contrast and beta estimate depends on the final design matrix.

visual.caption: FEAT displays the final EV columns and their temporal relationships.

scenes.narrationText: Inspect the design matrix after EV construction. Confirm that each column has the expected timing and order. Look for near-duplicate patterns or strong correlation. When predictors overlap, each beta estimate describes a contribution after accounting for the other columns.

display.title: Do not copy the stimulus list
display.body: The design should represent hypothesized causes of variation, not every available label.

items.label: Name the process
items.detail: What variation should this EV capture?

items.label: Define the timing
items.detail: How does the process unfold across the run?

items.label: State the contrast
items.detail: Which EV combination answers the hypothesis?

scenes.narrationText: A complex stimulus does not automatically require a column for every feature. Build the model around the hypothesized processes and comparisons. An EV is justified by the scientific question and design, not merely by the availability of a label.

sourceRefs.note: Complex models should be justified by underlying processes

scenes.narrationText: An EV is one hypothesized source of variation in the design matrix. Define what it represents, distinguish effects of interest from nuisance structure, and inspect its timing and relationship to other columns before interpreting beta estimates or contrasts.

sourceRefs.note: GLM columns, contrasts, and nuisance regressors

videos.title: The HRF and convolution
videos.description: Turn event timing into a delayed BOLD predictor by convolving neural-event estimates with a hemodynamic response model.

display.title: The blood response arrives late
display.body: Convolution turns brief event timing into a delayed, smooth model predictor.

scenes.narrationText: Neural events are fast, but the BOLD response is delayed and smooth. The hemodynamic response function, or HRF, approximates that response shape. Convolution combines event timing with the HRF to create a predictor that the GLM can compare with measured BOLD signal.

display.title: Apply the response at every event
display.body: Overlapping responses add together to form the expected BOLD pattern.

scenes.narrationText: Imagine placing a copy of the HRF at every event onset. Each copy is scaled by the event amplitude, shifted in time, and added to the others. The result is a continuous predictor. Closely spaced events produce overlapping responses, which is why timing affects estimation.

display.title: Rise, peak, fall, undershoot
display.body: A canonical HRF is a model of BOLD dynamics, not a measured neural waveform.

scenes.narrationText: A canonical response begins rising after roughly two seconds, peaks near five seconds, and may show a later undershoot. Those numbers are useful approximations, not universal constants. The HRF models vascular dynamics associated with neural activity; it is not the neural event itself.

display.title: Real HRFs vary
display.body: Latency and shape differ across people, brain regions, and physiological conditions.

scenes.narrationText: The canonical HRF is a practical model, but real responses vary across participants and regions. Basis functions or finite impulse response models can represent some variation. The appropriate choice depends on the hypothesis, design, and available data.

Convolution translates event timing into an expected BOLD pattern by applying the HRF at each event. Read the predictor as a model of delayed vascular response, and keep biological variability and design overlap in mind when interpreting the fit.

videos.title: Confound regressors
videos.description: Model structured nuisance variation such as motion and drift without pretending that regression can repair every data-quality problem.

display.title: Not every pattern is the task
display.body: Confound regressors model structured variation that is not the effect of interest.

scenes.narrationText: Measured BOLD contains task-related variation and many other patterns. Confound regressors represent structured nuisance variation, such as head motion or slow drift, so the GLM does not attribute all shared change to the task. They reduce some bias; they do not repair every artifact.

sourceRefs.note: Sources and spatial distribution of noise

display.title: Task and nuisance columns coexist
display.body: Each beta is estimated after accounting for the other columns in the design.

scenes.narrationText: Task and nuisance regressors enter the same design matrix but support different interpretations. The task columns estimate effects of interest. The nuisance columns absorb specified variation. Because the estimates are conditional, strong dependence between columns can change both precision and interpretation.

display.title: Plots reveal structured movement
display.body: Look for gradual drift, abrupt displacement, and movement aligned with the task.

visual.caption: The FEAT pre-stats report contains motion and preprocessing evidence to inspect before modeling.

scenes.narrationText: Motion parameters describe translation and rotation across the run. Inspect the plots for abrupt jumps, slow drift, and patterns synchronized with the task. A motion regressor can reduce linear shared variance, but task-correlated motion is especially difficult to separate.

display.title: Confounds cannot restore lost information
display.body: Missing coverage, severe distortion, spin-history effects, and corrupted volumes may remain unusable.

items.label: Inspect the images
items.detail: Motion estimates do not show every artifact.

items.label: Inspect task correlation
items.detail: Nuisance and effect columns may be inseparable.

items.label: Document exclusions
items.detail: Some runs or volumes may not support inference.

scenes.narrationText: Confound regression does not reconstruct missing anatomy or undo every motion artifact. Distortion can depend on position in the magnetic field, and spin-history effects can persist after realignment. Severe problems may require censoring, exclusion, or a revised acquisition—not another regressor.

Confound regressors help separate specified nuisance variation from task effects. Inspect the nuisance patterns, their relationship to the task, and the underlying images. A cleaner model does not automatically mean the original data became valid.

videos.title: Reviewing a complete FEAT report
videos.description: Review a completed FEAT report as an ordered chain of preprocessing, registration, design, and inferential evidence.

display.title: Results depend on every earlier step
display.body: Review inputs and transformations before interpreting a statistical map.

scenes.narrationText: A completed FEAT report is not automatically a valid analysis. It is a chain of evidence. Review motion and preprocessing first, registration second, the design and contrasts third, and statistical inference last. A failure early in the chain limits every later conclusion.

display.title: The report is a dependency map
display.body: Each section answers a different quality-control question.

visual.caption: The FEAT report links preprocessing, registration, design, and statistical output.

scenes.narrationText: Begin with pre-stats and ask whether motion, masking, and preprocessing outputs are plausible. Continue to registration and inspect anatomical correspondence. Then examine the design matrix, EVs, and contrasts. Only after those dependencies pass should you interpret thresholded results.

display.title: Specific observations are auditable
display.body: Replace “looks fine” with evidence about motion, boundaries, timing, and contrast direction.

visual.caption: Registration should be evaluated across multiple slices and anatomical boundaries.

scenes.narrationText: For motion, describe the pattern and any abrupt displacement. For registration, name boundaries and locations that agree or fail. For design, match columns to timing files and contrast weights to the hypothesis. Specific observations can be reviewed; vague reassurance cannot.

display.title: A z-statistic is not an effect size
display.body: Keep estimated effect, uncertainty, standardized evidence, and thresholded display distinct.

scenes.narrationText: A cope is the estimated contrast effect. A varcope describes uncertainty in that estimate. A t or z statistic standardizes evidence relative to uncertainty. A thresholded map shows locations surviving the chosen inferential procedure. Do not describe a z-statistic map as an effect-size map.

display.title: Pass, concern, or fail—with evidence
bullets: Link claims to the analysis plan

scenes.narrationText: Finish with an explicit quality-control judgment: pass, concern, or fail, followed by the observations that support it. Record limitations and their likely effect on interpretation. The goal is not to prove that FEAT finished; it is to decide what this run can defensibly support.

sourceRefs.note: Reverse inference, circularity, and analytic flexibility
